name: Amitriptyline
metabolism: CYP2C19 demethylation forms active nortriptyline; CYP2D6 hydroxylation supports further how fast the body clears it.
summary: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant used mainly for major depressive disorder and several pain syndromes. Common side effects include dry mouth, drowsiness, dizziness, constipation, and weight gain.
toxicities: Label-listed adverse reactions include drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, orthostatic hypotension, syncope, and cardiac conduction changes.

Tricyclic antidepressant overdose can be fatal. Critical manifestations include cardiac dysrhythmias, severe hypotension, convulsions, and CNS depression/coma; QRS widening and QT prolongation are important toxicity indicators.

Other serious risks include suicidal thoughts or behavior in younger patients, serotonin syndrome with interacting serotonergic drugs, and withdrawal symptoms after abrupt cessation of prolonged treatment.
generalRisks: The label warns that tricyclic antidepressant overdose may be fatal and can rapidly cause dysrhythmias, severe hypotension, seizures, coma, and respiratory/CNS depression. It also warns of suicidality in children, adolescents, and young adults; anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension/falls, impaired driving, serotonin syndrome with interacting drugs, and withdrawal symptoms after abrupt cessation. MAOIs and cisapride are contraindicated concomitant drugs.
saferUse: Treat suspected overdose as an emergency even if symptoms are not yet obvious; the label calls for prompt hospital monitoring after suspected tricyclic overdose.
Do not combine with MAOIs or cisapride. Avoid alcohol and use caution with barbiturates and other CNS depressants.

Do not drive or operate machinery if alertness or coordination is impaired. Do not abruptly stop prolonged treatment; discuss dose reduction with the prescriber. Monitor for worsening mood or suicidal thoughts, especially early in treatment or after dose changes.
dosageRemark: The label gives prescription treatment dosing for depression only. No evidence-based recreational dose thresholds or duration are established here, so none are entered.
